articles.title: Main Hall - Finding the Artist Walkthrough - Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Guide - IGN
articles.summary: This is a continuation of IGN's walkthrough for Castlevania: Belmont's Curse. In this section, we'll be focusing on the Main Hall as we explore
articles.body:
This is a continuation of IGN's walkthrough for Castlevania: Belmont's Curse . In this section, we'll be focusing on the Main Hall as we explore it to find the Artist, the next boss, and Tarot, which you'll be unlocking after having explored sections of the Clock Tower to find The Builder , known as Talos . You can follow along with this playthrough to review the previous sections here .

You'll be starting this portion of the walkthrough after leaving the Ferryman's Wharf in the Main Hall and entering the Grand Hall.

From the Grand Hall, you'll be making your way up, partially repeating the path you took to the Clock Tower, returning to the Watch Tower as you want to unlock the door at the top of the West Tower. Unfortunately, you'll need to repeat the Watch Tower climbing puzzle to reach the top and then get to the right side, making your way down. For those who'd like a refresher on how to scale the left portion, here's a full breakdown.

At the base of the Watch Tower, you'll only have one pathway to go, and that's up. Expect to encounter multiple spike traps, shards, and jumps that you have to do. If you fail anywhere along this path, until you reach the top, you'll respawn back at the bottom.

For the first portion, jump into the floating painting and wait for it to reach the left side. Jump up from there, and aim for the purple anchor on your right. You won't have long, though, as you'll need to jump to the left wall, or go straight to the floating painting above. You can take a break here, but when you're ready, you'll need to jump directly up, immediately activating your Halo to bypass the abyss shards, before turning them off to land safely on the platform.

Now, you need to activate your Halo and jump to the left, bypassing the wall and deactivating it again to safely rest on the shards, or go into the pit of spikes. This can take some time and practice to get correctly, as your timing needs to be precise.

From here, keep your Halo off, and wall leap up to the top. When you reach the right path, activate the Halo and bypass the wall, where you'll find a breakaway platform and a floating painting above you. You may need to jump onto the abyss shards wall to your left as you wait for the floating painting to reach you before you can take it.

After that, wait until it reaches the left side, and then shoot up, jumping onto the wall on your left and using the yellow anchor to swing to the right, landing at the foot of the glowing door.

Now, rather than going through the glowing door, go through the floating portrait that appears next to it. Wait until it reaches the bottom of this wall, and then fling yourself to the right side. Fall down the wall, where you'll land on a floating platform. You only have a few seconds to jump onto the next floating painting. If you don't have enough time, cling to the wall to the left to hold yourself up and buy time.

When you're in the second floating painting, fling yourself down onto a platform of shards. When you're ready, jump from this platform and activate your Halo, going through this wall of shards. There's nothing for you to land on, unfortunately, but the floating painting down here is not moving, so you don't have to worry about timing. Just don't expect a platform to catch you.

You can then fling yourself directly downward, landing on a breakable platform. You won't have long to grab and throw yourself into the floating painting on the right side, preventing you from being caught by the spikes. You can jump over to this side and use the whip to throw yourself into the painting, rather than waiting on the left side.

Now, when the floating painting reaches the bottom, throw yourself to the left, and you'll land safely at the end of this puzzle. You can now go through the glowing door below you and advance.

However, if you want to unlock the weapon chest to your right (the gold one), you can hit the lever that's to your left of the glowing grate, and the lever at the end is available. You can reach it by going down through the glowing door and hitting the lever in the West Hall, unlocking the wall that was previously blocking you from this section.

Return to the base of the Watch Tower, and you'll be able to unlock the door blocking the golden chest. The trick is that now you're on a timer, with the lever at the base slowly going back to its original position and shutting the door. You have to repeat the puzzle we've just gone through to reach the golden chest in time. You can't make any mistakes as you're navigating this puzzle, or you'll have to start over again.

When you pass through the wall, the lever stops, and you'll have completed the puzzle. You'll receive the Rapiers, the Refined dual blades for the rest of the playthrough.

Now, make your way through the top of the West Door, and you'll enter the Elevator Tower and a Mirror of Life. Head to the right to access the Mirror of Life, unlocking it for this section of the castle.

Before going further down this side, return to the elevator in the Elevator Room if you haven't already accessed it, and take it to the top. You'll unlock the one at the bottom, next to the Clock Tower entrance. You'll now be able to avoid the Watch Tower puzzle in the future.

Now, back to the Elevator Tower's Mirror of Life, follow the right path and you'll enter the upper portion of the Grand Hall. Take the path to the right, and you'll enter an encounter at the central section, where you find the flying knights for the first time. These flying knights are similar in appearance to the ones with the lances, but they carry a large shield, with a different type of weapon. Dispatching them requires you to use your whip to close the distance, or you can use the Fist of Talos (which is one of the Works of Mercy) to eliminate them while they're in the air.

Along with the flying knights, expect to fight the other knights that are also stationed around you. Once you've dealt with them, you'll find that there are several floating paintings in this room. There's one you can reach on the left side, next to the entrance you used to enter this area. Use it to land on the platform to your left, and destroy the XP statue.

With that added to your XP pool, head to the bottom right of this section of the Grand Hall, and there's a lower section that you can enter, highlighted by the purple anchor under a grate. Fall down here, and you'll enter a narrow hallway with a trap panel in front of you. You won't be able to dodge it, forcing fireballs to appear behind and above you, along with multiple bloodsucking ghouls in front of you.

You'll need to do your best to dodge these fireballs as best you can, potentially dodging underneath the enemies so they get hit by them, and make it to the other end of the hallway. Jump down, and you'll enter the lower section of this part of the Grand Hall. As you arrive at the bottom, there's a section to the left with another XP statue that you can destroy.

Now, head to the center of the room, and you'll find a knight with a pair of boomerang-throwing skeletons on either side. Defeat the knight, and a floating eyeball appears. Once they're all taken care of, head to the right side and destroy the XP statue next to the painting of Alucard. You can then jump down from this grate and head to the right, going through the glowing door to enter the Old Gallery.

You'll find one of Dracula's statues at the entrance. Interact with it, and the statue reveals that the Alucard paintings are much more than mere mentions of Dracula's son, but they point to secrets hidden throughout the Main Hall. This also unlocks another Arcana Clue surrounding the Artist.

You can use the Alucard painting next to the statue as a good test. Leap down directly from the painting, and you'll discover a lower section below that was previously hidden, and a new doorway for you to explore.

Although you can go through and explore this door, this is an optional area, and one that you do not need to go down to defeat the Artist.

Confirming that the Alucard paintings are true, you'll see these appear all over your map throughout the Grand Hall. We'll be making our way back through some areas and providing opportunities to grab them. For now, focus on the Old Gallery. Return to the Alucard painting above you, and proceed to the right.

You'll find a massive pile of spikes and a floating painting barely out of reach, with fireballs shooting downward in between you. Wait for the fireballs to go off before jumping and throwing yourself into the painting.

The painting will go to the right side, and then you can fling yourself up into the upper floor, where you'll find a new enemy. It's a floating sword that conjures additional swords around it to protect it, and damages you if you get too close. The trick is to damage the swords around it before you engage the larger one, but the middle sword does summon more over time. I've found that the Holy Cross or the Fist of Talos are an excellent way to make short work of these swords.

Once you've dealt with it, head to the left, and you'll find a permanent Attack upgrade, increasing your overall damage.

Return to the Alucard sword, and head back to the Grand Hall. There's an Alucard painting immediately after this entrance, pointing downward. Head below, and you'll find the lower section, the middle area of the Grand Hall. At the center of this narrow hallway is a massive gear (with a few ghouls on the left side).

Hit the gear to cause it to move, and you'll open the walls that were blocking these sections off, connecting the entire Grand Hall to each part, making it much easier to travel throughout this area.

Before you head back to the upper Grand Hall section, follow this hallway to the left and continue through the glowing door. This will take you to Brauner's Atelier, the boss room for the Artist. In this lower section, there's a large gear you need to hit (like the one from the Grand Hall) to open up the doors.

Inside, Rose asks Medusa if the statue is one of her creations. She confirms it is not, and is a creation by the Artist. When you approach the statue, you'll receive the final Arcana clue surrounding the Artist, revealing that he has put a warning on it for Talos, saying that he will swoop in if he dares attempt to destroy this masterpiece statue he's created, which is the perfect opportunity to bring him to you!

You can use the floating paintings to reach the middle of the room, and throw yourself upward to the purple anchor. When you reach the purple anchor, throw yourself down using Talos' smash, and land directly on it, summoning the Artist.

The Artist appears and has a brief exchange with Rose, revealing his true identity to be Brauner. Rose calls his masterpiece a hunk of rock, and Brauner is more than happy to engage Rose in combat given her rude comment.

However, unlike the other boss encounters you've had, Brauner is not a fighter. He gives up without putting up much of a fight, and willingly gives Rose his Arcana power. Rose absorbs him into her Tarot cards, adding one more power to her abilities.

With Brauner's ability, you'll be able to summon gargoyles and have them aid you in battle, as they spit fireballs and float around you.

Although Brauner is more than keen to assist Rose in defeating Dracula, he does not provide a good context of where to go next.

With Brauner's ability acquired, you can return to the Grand Hall, as there are additional Tarot cards that you need to unlock, and the next one is for The Occultist . They are in the Library.

You can find them by making your way to the upper part of the Grand Hall. In this upper section, there's a floating painting on the right side you can use, shooting you onto a platform on the right side and through a glowing door.

The doorway brings you to the Bridge of Knowledge. Follow it, and you'll find the entrance to the Library, the next area you need to explore to hunt down The Occulist.

articles.title: Defection Walkthrough - Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Guide - IGN
articles.summary: Capping off the marines' time in enemy territory after Stranded is the next main mission of MW4's campaign, Defection. Here, Ko and the squad put
articles.body:
Capping off the marines' time in enemy territory after Stranded is the next main mission of MW4's campaign , Defection. Here, Ko and the squad put their efforts from the previous mission to use to disable the North Korean airbase and escape with their lives.

When you take control of Park again in the truck, stand up and grab the HAN 86 assault rifle, some throwing knives, and the handgun on the seat if you’d like. But if you turn around, there’s a Astaroth .57 bolt-action sniper rifle with a thermal scope on the truck’s wall.

Leave the truck then follow park into the next room where you’ll take out two unaware enemies in tandem. Kal then kills the lights, and the next room has another pair of enemy soldiers to dispose of.

Plant Explosives on the Hypersonic Missiles

Go through the doors and plant explosive charges on the first vehicle target.

When you reach the second vehicle target, there are two more baddies on the right. Kal instructs you to plant charges first, then engage.

After doing so, continue further in until an enemy squad comes through the door - take them out, then turn left to plant charges on the third vehicle.

Head into the doors the enemy squad came out of and interact with the next set of double doors to trigger a cutscene with Ko and Ri.

You’re back in control of Park. Here you’ll engage with a lot of enemies, so be strategic about which weapons you use, and make sure you use cover and armor plates to stay alive. Kal and Moon are to your right ready to engage with you, as well as a nice collection of supplies; ammo, molotovs, bomb drones, and semtex.

When you’re ready, start blasting. Enemies come at you from all sides, but picking up the bomb drones and taking a group or two out from afar before they’re aware you’re there is recommended.

Find Jae on the map and hold Square to switch to his perspective to take on a sniper positon across from where Park and company are.

As Jae, look to your right to see a bunch of enemy soldiers shooting at Dunn and West at a rooftop from numerous anglers. Using your sniper, pick them off to ease the fire on your allies.

Trucks start approaching from the southeast, but they’re no match for the grenade launcher Jae has equipped. Turn around and blast the two trucks into oblivion before they can reach your allies.

Look for Dunn on the map back in the direction of the main action, and hold Square to swap to him.

As Dunn, you’ll need to take out the mortars firing on your position. There’s heavy enemy fire directly ahead of you, so take a quick second to shoot an RPG in that direction

Then turn your attention to the left where the enemy mortar team is firing from behind a truck. Take them out.

Truckloads of enemies start entering through the gate, so use Dunn’s RPG to make short work of them.

Swap back to Jae to use his grenade launcher to take out the three armored BMP tanks. Two blasts each should take care of them. Switch back to Dunn and take out the third with two RPG hits.

Swapping between Jae and Dunn, use their grenade launchers and RPG fire to take the helo out in a few hits. Make sure to switch often, as the helicopter will focus on whoever you’re controlling.

Fight your way across the airfield as a friendly helicopter arrives to provide you exfil. Make sure you actually take enemies out instead of just booking it straight to the extraction point, since they're still relentless at this point.

As the helicopter takes off, Park has a front row seat to seat setting off the explosives. Hold Square to send the enemies sky high, ending the mission.

articles.title: Attack on Titan 3: The Final Preview
articles.summary: Attack on Titan 3 may come with a number, but it isn’t a direct sequel in the truest sense of the word. It’s more of a retelling.  Based on my time with it, Attack on Titan 3 is juggling a lot of plates, and its ambition to do something new with the franchise is pretty laudable.
articles.body:
This isn’t a straight retelling of the anime, but it does follow the same overall storyline.

The designers aim to include something in combat for more advanced/experienced players too.

The moments in-between big battles are some of my favorites so far.

I must confess something before I get this preview started: I bowed out of Attack on Titan early. After the first season, actually. I didn’t think it was terrible or anything. I was there for the human drama. Little people swinging around like Spider-Man and dealing with their trauma while playing a game of David and Goliath against big, scary Titans. But when those little dudes started being able to become Titans, well… it just wasn’t for me. But after spending some time with Attack on Titan 3 and speaking to producer Hideo Suzuki, I’m tempted to give it another go… at least as a video game.

Attack on Titan 3 may come with a number, but it isn’t a direct sequel in the truest sense of the word. It’s more of a retelling. Part of that, Suzuki told me, was because it’s been seven years since Attack on Titan 2: Final Battle. “Right after the previous game, we already had started talking about the sequel, but at the time the anime series was still ongoing. So we were like, ‘What kind of concept should [the next one] be?’ And we did think about just covering the new parts of the anime series, but as a game or as a one product, we didn't think it was quite enough. So we were like, ‘Okay, one series is coming to an end, so why don't we just cover the story from beginning to the end and just kind of follow that storyline?’”

But Attack on Titan 3 isn’t just a straight retelling. You’ll be strapping on your ODM gear as an original character, but your backstory is interesting. After your squad is wiped out on your first mission as a squad leader, your character – I named mine John Titan, not knowing I could later choose their gender – is too traumatized (and afraid of fighting Titans) to continue. But since they also happen to be a great engineer and a generational talent with ODM gear, they’re kept on to fix things and train new recruits. It’s an interesting role to step into; games rarely ask you to embody deeply traumatized people who are so badly mentally broken that they have to step away from what they were great at.

Suzuki, however, told me that decision was intentional. “The reason that we had that kind of story in the beginning is we needed to establish that the Titans are the humans’ enemy. So the character goes to battle, he experiences the loss and trauma and then goes back with a stronger determination to fight Titans from then on. This time, the character is set up as a senior to Eren and other characters. And I mean, although he is a senior or more veteran trooper, if he's so strong from the beginning, there won't be much story to tell. So we have to have some kind of setback in the beginning for him to go through and it's that incident in the beginning. And then he's going to kind of play the role of Eren and others' mentor, but then they will work together and then they recover from the trauma and grow after.”

After playing with the character creator, I’m assigned to the 104th cadets, where I’ll be instructing Eren Jaeger, Armin Arlett, and Mikasa Ackerman, among others. My job, along with another hard-assed instructor named Keith, is to mold these kids into proper soldiers. But we have to break them first. You have to prepare the clay before you can shape it. But these recruits aren’t just blank slates. Like the show (and manga) it’s based on, Attack on Titan’s characters are their own people, sometimes to a fault. As soon as the initiation ceremony is over, Eren Jaeger bombards me with questions about why there aren’t more scouting missions and why we aren’t retaking the walls, and I’m forced to watch as my character relives their own shame. It’s a neat moment.

But I have to get to know these kids, too. Attack on Titan is probably most famous for its high-flying human vs. Titan battles or its knock down, drag out Titan-on-Titan brawls, but it’s a human story at heart, and building relationships with the other characters is a core part of Attack on Titan 3.

“There are many ways that the player can build a friendship with anime characters, and one of them is giving gifts to them,” Suzuki tells me later. “A second one is to eat together in a mess hall, and also they can invite those characters into their room and have conversations. So by pleasing the other characters, they can build rapport, a better friendship, and then it will affect the combat… These comrades that you build friendships with, you can invite them or you can take them onto these exterior missions or exterior scouts. And outside of the wall, you of course have battles against Titans and the player and those characters can work together to carry out special skills. We call these Buddy Arts… So the better relationship you have with these other characters… the better that your exterior missions or scouts are going to get.”

First, though, I have to whip them into fighting shape, and that means learning how to use the ODM gear. Grappling to rocks and trees before flinging yourself to the next place is a blast, and it feels like you have a lot of control over every aspect of movement. There are several features that are new to the series, like the ability to anchor yourself to buildings or trees, precisely control your altitude, or even slide under arches. When I asked him about redesigning the ODM gear, Suzuki told me that they wanted to make sure they were keeping pace with how games had evolved since Attack on Titan 2, but also offer something for more advanced players. “I think in the previous game, it was pretty playable for people who are not advanced game players, but in this one we wanted to have those advanced players to play better, battle better, and have a more sense of achievement when they defeat the Titans.

“But improving the ODM wasn’t enough,” Suzuki told me. The Titans have to improve with it because the team at Omega Force wanted those fights to feel suitably meaningful and epic. “In the previous game, the range of [ODM] control that you had was pretty narrow, and at the same time it was kind of simpler and easy for all players across the board. And this one, the base is still simple… but this time you had more control over a lot of the actions that you take and then you can really narrow down your tactics accordingly… but then that wasn't enough. If ODM only gets better, then the Titans are not going to be as threatening to the players. So we had to evolve the Titans as well. So their systems, for example, their algorithm and battle patterns, we definitely improved those too. And so they're still threatening Titans and they're big obstacles [for] the humans.”

I finally get my first crack at one after I jump to a later point in the story. I have to cleave through some human enemies, but they’re not too terrible, and it helps me get a feel for actual combat before taking on a Titan: the War Hammer Titan, to be exact, and it’s a bear of a fight. Unlike the Titan I fought earlier on in the game’s tutorial, I can’t damage it directly. Instead, I have to wear it down by filling up its Break Gauge before I can go in for the kill. Fighting efficiently means dodging and parrying attacks while getting my own licks in, but it’s more of a battle of patience than anything else. I’m like a mosquito fighting an elephant; I gotta take it down a bite at a time, and it’ll take them a lot less effort to squash me than it would for me to cause him meaningful harm.

Thankfully, I have the tools. I just have to manage them. Healing Tonics top me off when he smacks me around, new blades replace old ones when they dull and no longer make a dent, and Combat Arts deal more damage when I do enough damage to earn them. By far the coolest ones, though, are the Buddy Arts, which are flashy as hell. I feel slick every time I pull one off. Even with them, though, the fight is a matter of endurance. I almost make it, but I falter at the end. Not bad for a mosquito.

What I played of Attack on Titan 3’s battles felt memorable, but what stuck with me after my demo ended was all the time I spent out of combat with the other characters of this world. It makes the fights against the Titans hit harder than it would if they were happening all the time. “That was very much intentional,” Suzuki told me when I asked him about it. “This IP can be all battles. I mean, no one's going to complain about that, but because the anime characters are so attractive, they have so much depth. So to show their daily lives will probably make the fans happy… In manga and anime too, there are a lot of comical moments and events. So there's [a] tension-and-release kind of relationship. I think that makes the game more enjoyable.”

Suzuki told me that he hopes introducing a new character will help old fans see the story in a different way and introduce new players to Attack on Titan, but Attack on Titan 3 doesn’t just recreate the anime. There’s plenty of new stuff for them to discover, too. “We do have some original content as well, so we have a lot of sub stories and events. And we don't really say this out loud in interviews and stuff, but… we actually put so many of these sub-stories and events in this particular title and we work very closely with Kodansha, the IP holder. And so I want the players to enjoy every single bit of that.”

Suzuki also let drop one more detail for fans to look forward to as we wrapped up: "We've already announced that the opening anime sequence will be produced by Mappa. They're the creator of the anime. And this I have not said anywhere yet, but I watched the work in progress version of the opening movie and the quality is just phenomenal. So I really want the players to look forward to that.”

Based on my time with it, Attack on Titan 3 is juggling a lot of plates, and its ambition to do something new with the franchise is pretty laudable. Will it make me an Attack on Titan guy? Who knows? But I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t curious to put on my ODM gear one more time and help my character complete their quest for redemption. You can’t hide from the worst moments of your life, but you can choose how you face them, and who you face them with. Either way, you’ve got to learn to live with them, and fight your demons (and Titans) head on.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Will Borger is an IGN freelancer. You can find him on Bluesky @edgarallanbro.

articles.title: Essential Combat Tips for Phantom Blade Zero - Phantom Blade Zero Guide - IGN
articles.summary: Being a master swordsman in Phantom Blade Zero takes more than just swinging your blade around and somersaulting every time someone takes a swing at you.
articles.body:
Being a master swordsman in Phantom Blade Zero takes more than just swinging your blade around and somersaulting every time someone takes a swing at you. There’s nuance to this, details that can make the difference between whether it's your head, or that of your opponents that goes rolling. That’s why we’ve put together these tips and tricks to help you master combat in Phantom Blade Zero.

Essential Combat Tips for Phantom Blade Zero

Years of action games like Ninja Gaiden or Dark Souls have taught players the value of dodging, blocking, and hitting back in the windows in between. However, that’s not typically the best approach here. Instead, most of your defense should come via parries.

That means timing button taps when attacks land, not holding it down and waiting. Not only does this keep you safe, it’s also often the best way to chip away at an enemy's sha-chi meter, breaking their guard and opening them up to attacks. For tougher enemies, especially bosses, this is your window to do meaningful damage. Ideally, you are looking for the flash of sparks that lets you know you’ve timed your parry perfectly.

Soul can carve through basic enemies without too much trouble. However, tougher baddies and bosses lie in wait to make his day much worse, and they won’t be impressed with a few basic attacks.

Really putting the hurt on them comes down to timing. Use your attacks and parries to break down the enemies guard first, go all out on the aggression. A particularly effective damage phase will look something like this: Guard is broken and you consume your Sha-Chi essence, then you empty your sha-chi meter with your Sha-Chi attacks, switch weapons, and use your now refilled sha-chi to do it again until the enemy stagger ends.

Fights against tough enemies, especially bosses, are as much about managing your sha-chi meter as they are about your quick-twitch combat skills. You need to keep your meter up, when it runs empty you are exposed to a lot of potential damage. Follow the 30% rule, as long as your Sha-chi is greater than 30%, swing freely, including using your sha-chi attacks. However, once it drops below that threshold, focus on just standard attacks until it refills. The exceptions are when you are pummeling a guard broken enemy like we mentioned before, or when you are about to switch weapons, which will instantly refill your sha-chi.

Always have one shieldbreaker phantom edge equipped

While Soul has an extensive arsenal, you only get to use four weapons, two standard and two phantom edges, in a single fight. Use whatever tools of destruction you like, no judgement here, but do yourself a favor and make sure to always have at least one Phantom Edge that specializes in breaking down shields. Shielded enemies will appear fairly regularly, and most standard weapons will take forever to break through their guard. But, if you have something like Dread Axe, or Iron Gauntlets equipped, you can smash through them almost instantly, saving a lot of time and effort against harder targets.

One of the early upgrades to Soul is called Flowing Chi. The description lists a bunch of requirements, but all you need to know is that this is unlimited free usage of your Phantom Edges , in the right context. Once you have this ability, you will start seeing a new button prompt appear. Tap it quick enough, and Soul will bust out an attack from a phantom edge, without consuming any Remnant Spark. When the prompt appears and what attack is used depends on the enemy, and whether or not you’ve unlocked the weapon used in the combo, but it can add a powerful effect to the middle of your assault. You can even get an item that grants a chance to generate new Remnant Spark anytime you use these free attacks.

Jagged Steel is a top tier weapon you get early, upgrade it right away

Early on you’ll face a boss called Jagged Steel, the Frenzied Brute . Cut him down to get his sword, also called Jagged Steel . You’ll unlock the ability to upgrade weapons soon, and make this your top priority; it’s by far one of the most powerful early-game weapons you can get your hands on. It has a great moveset, deals solid damage, and builds up a status effect called bleed, dealing a large chunk of additional damage when it procs. Get this to level five as soon as you can to unlock a special attack that builds bleep quickly on guard-broken enemies, and thank us later.

Another great weapon available in the early hours is the Scarlet Wraithblade. However, unlike Jagged Edge, this is on an optional boss, and completely missable. Don’t miss it. This massive two-handed sword cleaves through enemies quickly. It also leaves a wake of red lilies behind, which drain the sha-chi and health of any enemy standing in them, including bosses. Given how important draining sha-chi is to set up your attack opportunities, that’s a huge benefit.

To get the Scarlet Wraithblade, you’ll need to reach the Sha-chi tower in the Weeping Creek Valley, which you'll come across naturally as part of the story during Steel and Steam . After dealing with the monks on the first floor, look for an opening in the floor, slide down, and follow the path to the left to find Hua, Deadly Betrothed. You’ll need to beat her to get this sword. Be warned though, she’s no pushover. Check out our detailed Hua boss fight guide for help.

Soul gets access to a wide variety of accessories over his travels, and can eventually equip up to six of them at a time to maximize his combat potential. The game will often telegraph what sort of enemies you will be facing based on what accessories it drops, like giving you the Cavalrybane, right before you take on a particularly nasty jerk on horseback. As a general rule of thumb, if you get a new accessory specific to a type of enemy, or negating a type of damage, consider equipping it sooner rather than later.

Still, some accessories are good in almost any situation. Here are a few of our favorites.

The Token of Pursuit increases damage to Guard-Broken enemies. Since that’s when you’ll deal most of your damage, that’s an easy winner.

The Quick Hand Pendant and Quick Hand Might boost your damage with one and two-handed weapons respectively. That’s especially useful if you are doubling up on either weapon type.

The Mother’s Talisman restores some of your HP when your guard is broken. While we don’t suggest spending a lot of time in this state, if you are clever with your weapon switching, you can leverage this for some badly needed mid-fight healing.

The Reflex Device increases the timing window for your dodges and parries. Fully upgraded it gives a 25% boost. That’s a pretty big difference, and, with how much you’ll be using those moves, it can be a literal game changer with those tight windows.

It’s a dangerous world out there, but if you follow these tips you can turn the tables and become the danger yourself.

articles.title: How to Start the Charting the Unknown DLC (All Requirements) - Crimson Desert Guide - IGN
articles.summary: The first Crimson Desert DLC, Charting the Unknown, introduces several new questlines alongside shipbuilding that may have you wondering how to start them.
articles.body:
The first Crimson Desert DLC, Charting the Unknown, introduces several new questlines alongside shipbuilding that may have you wondering how to start them. We've included how far you'll need to get to get your first ship, how to continue the story of Kliff, Damiane, and Oongka, as well as plenty of other helpful info. Such as how to start the Garden of Trials as well!

How to Start the Shipbuilding and Ocean Questline

Before you can start sailing in Charting the Unknown, you'll need to progress the Greymanes Faction Quests . This requires completing the Gathered Will quest chain under Grounds of the Sunrise . The final quest you'll need to finish in that section is Expanding the Camp . Not to be confused with a previous quest of the same name under Embers of Return.

Upon completing the right one, you'll then have access to a new Greymanes Faction Quest category, Chartering the Unknown. This has a total of 14 quests, with three quest chains immediately available: A Wider World, Shield of Hernand, and Renewed Vitality. These will get you to owning your first small ship, until you can build or purchase a larger ship.

With that said, you'll need a lot of Camp Funds to get a bigger ship. For example, a large ship costs 6,000,000 Camp Funds.

To continue the main story and learn more about Kliff, Damiane, and Oongka, you'll need to complete the original main questline first . After finishing Epilogue: Journey's End and starting Crimson Desert with the DLC, Charting the Unknown, you'll have three new questlines available.

Make sure to play as the relevant character for each quest in the table below before trying to start them. Otherwise, you won't be able to work on that quest chain.

If you want to challenge yourself and experience the boss rush added in the Chartering the Unknown DLC, Garden of Trials, you'll need to finish the main story first. Fortunately, this doesn't require completing any of the Chartering the Unknown story quests previously mentioned. Once you've finished the questline in the original story, Epilogue: Journey's End, you'll be able to unlock it.

Make your way to the Axiom Archive in the Abyss , directly above the Town of Hernand. You'll also find it inside The Path of Providence when looking at the Abyss on your map. Travel there and then head toward the building straight ahead of the Abyss Nexus to trigger a cutscene.

Upon approaching the archive, a cutscene will trigger that transports you to the Garden of Trials. Continue forward, where you'll find many short pillars with cubes resting on them. You can then step on a pad near a trial to examine the cube there. As long as you've defeated these bosses previously, you'll be able to challenge them back-to-back without any consumables.

articles.title: Death Stranding Isolations Anime Gets First Trailer
articles.summary: Kojima Productions revealed the first trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an original anime series set in the world of Death Stranding, scheduled to release on Disney+ next year.
articles.body:
Kojima Productions revealed the first trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an original anime series set in the world of Death Stranding , scheduled to release on Disney+ next year.

The news was shared in a tweet late on October 29 (the morning of October 30 in Japan). In the trailer, a girl with blonde hair is roused from sleep by dreams of being consumed by the tar.

The tweet itself doesn't provide any more clarity; in the post, a quote reads, "My mom became a crater."

DEATH STRANDING ISOLATIONS Teaser Trailer & New Details Revealed! "My mom became a crater." An all-new animated series set in the world of DEATH STRANDING, featuring an original story driven by its own unique ensemble of characters. Streaming exclusively on Disney+ in 2027! Directed by Takayuki Sano Series Composition & Screenplay by Tow Ubukata Animated by E&H production #DeathStranding #DeathStrandingIsolations — KOJIMA PRODUCTIONS (Eng) (@KojiPro2015_EN) October 30, 2026

DEATH STRANDING ISOLATIONS Teaser Trailer & New Details Revealed! "My mom became a crater." An all-new animated series set in the world of DEATH STRANDING, featuring an original story driven by its own unique ensemble of characters. Streaming exclusively on Disney+ in 2027! Directed by Takayuki Sano Series Composition & Screenplay by Tow Ubukata Animated by E&H production #DeathStranding #DeathStrandingIsolations

Death Stranding Isolations is promised to be an original story driven by its "own unique ensemble of characters," suggesting that Sam Porter Bridges, Fragile, and co. won't be major players in the narrative.

As previously announced , the series will stream exclusively on Disney+ in 2027, though no exact date was given. The anime is directed by Takayuki Sano, known for doing the key animation, as well as designing creatures and props, directing, and many other duties for a swath of major anime over the years. Most notably, he served as the animation director for Attack on Titan's final season, as well as episodes of Jujutsu Kaisen and the movie Jujutsu Kaisen 0.

Tow Ubukata is set to write the series' screenplay. Ubukata is a noted science-fiction author who lent his talents to Psycho-Pass 3 and Psycho-Pass: Providence, Ghost in the Shell: The New Movie, and was the Free Scenario Plotter for Shenmue.

E&H production are animating the series, best known for their work on Undead Unluck: Winter Arc, Ninja Kamui, and the 2026 Magic Knight Rayearth reboot.

Kojima also unveiled a new poster for his upcoming horror game in collaboration with director Jordan Peele, OD Knock , showing Sophia Lillis looking up at a long, red object above her.

This is the latest news from Kojima after the game director expressed an intention to make cameos in films and TV, with an appearance in a "big" live-action film coming up. His studio's next big action espionage game, Physint, was also in the news recently after changing hands from Sony to Xbox . Thus far, details on this game are still sparse, but Kojima has confirmed a few cast members in Bill Skarsgard , Charlie Fraser and Minami Hamabe.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: Valkyries most to blame for ugly WNBA Finals Game 6 loss vs. Dream
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries had an opportunity to secure their first WNBA championship Thursday afternoon. Instead, a disastrous first quarter put them in a h...
articles.body:
The Golden State Valkyries had an opportunity to secure their first WNBA championship Thursday afternoon. Instead, a disastrous first quarter put them in a hole they could never quite climb out of.

Golden State fell 80-69 to the Atlanta Dream in Game 6 of the WNBA Finals , setting up a winner-take-all Game 7 on Saturday in San Francisco. Despite a late comeback attempt, the Valkyries could not overcome a 20-point halftime deficit as Atlanta forced the series back to Golden State.

The Valkyries entered Thursday's matchup having won two consecutive games, but looked nothing like the team that had taken control of the series. Atlanta's offense came alive early, while Golden State struggled to generate much of anything on the other end.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

So who deserves the most blame for the Valkyries' missed opportunity to close out the WNBA Finals?

Golden State's biggest problem Thursday was apparent almost immediately. The Valkyries simply did not look prepared to match the intensity of an Atlanta team fighting to keep its championship hopes alive.

The Dream shot 11-of-15 from the field and 6-of-8 from beyond the arc in the opening quarter, building a commanding 32-15 advantage. Atlanta had already matched its entire first-half scoring output from Game 5 just six and a half minutes into Thursday's contest.

Some of that can be attributed to the Dream making difficult shots, but Golden State's defense also failed to establish the physicality that had been so important throughout its postseason run.

Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase deserves some criticism for her team's slow start. Golden State was one win away from a championship, yet looked overwhelmed by Atlanta's aggressiveness on both ends of the floor.

The unusual 12:30 p.m. Thursday tipoff could have disrupted the teams' normal routines, but that is hardly an excuse. Both teams were dealing with the same circumstances, and Atlanta had no trouble finding its rhythm.

Golden State eventually made adjustments, particularly with its defensive pressure in the second half. But those changes came far too late.

Nakase has guided the Valkyries to within one win of a championship. Still, her team's inability to come out prepared for arguably its biggest game of the season deserves scrutiny.

Valkyries' defense had no answer for Atlanta's early shooting

Golden State's defense has been one of the biggest reasons for its success throughout the Finals. Unfortunately, that defensive identity was almost nonexistent during Thursday's opening quarter.

Allisha Gray finished with 23 points, while Rhyne Howard added 21 as Atlanta repeatedly capitalized on Golden State's defensive breakdowns. Angel Reese also added 15 points and 13 rebounds, giving the Dream another productive offensive option .

The Valkyries allowed Atlanta to score 46 points in the first half, a particularly disappointing showing considering the Dream had managed just 55 points in their Game 5 loss.

Veronica Burton acknowledged Golden State's defensive shortcomings following the game.

"They scored 32 points in the first quarter. That's unacceptable on our end," Burton said, as reported by Kenzo Fukuda of ClutchPoints. "Got to play better defense. Obviously, they're hitting good shots and getting good looks. I think we were sped up a little bit, but we cleaned it up in the other quarters defensively."

Golden State deserves credit for eventually tightening things up. The Dream scored just 34 points across the final three quarters, and the Valkyries managed to make the game somewhat competitive down the stretch.

But championship-caliber defense cannot disappear for an entire quarter, especially against an opponent facing elimination.

Gabby Williams pointed to ball pressure and physicality as areas Golden State must improve heading into Game 7.

"You set the tone with the physicality," Williams said. "I think when you punch first, when you are aggressive at the beginning and you try to be later, well, that's when fouls start getting called."

The Valkyries ultimately allowed Atlanta to dictate the pace early, and that proved costly.

While Golden State's defense deserves plenty of blame, its offense did little to help matters.

The Valkyries managed just 26 points in the first half, shooting a dismal 9-of-34 from the field. Atlanta's defensive pressure disrupted Golden State's offensive sets, forcing difficult attempts and preventing the Valkyries from establishing any consistent rhythm.

Williams finished with a game-high 26 points, but needed 22 field-goal attempts to get there, making just eight. Tiffany Hayes added 15 points, though Golden State struggled to find enough offensive production elsewhere to keep pace with Atlanta.

The Valkyries were particularly ineffective at attacking the basket early, allowing the Dream to control the game while Golden State settled into an inefficient offensive performance.

That changed somewhat in the second half, when Golden State became more aggressive getting to the rim and drawing fouls.

The Valkyries eventually cut Atlanta's lead to eight points late in the fourth quarter, an impressive turnaround considering they had trailed by as many as 25.

However, missed opportunities around the basket and the enormous early deficit left little room for error.

There is something to be said for Golden State's refusal to quit. The Valkyries could have folded after falling behind by 20 at halftime, but instead fought their way back into the contest.

Still, the late rally should not overshadow how poorly they executed offensively for much of the afternoon.

Golden State now has one final opportunity to secure its first WNBA championship Saturday.

Reporting by Charles Odum of The Associated Press was used in preparing this piece.

articles.title: The Hollow Day 8: Floor 8 Maze and the Sonaria Quest Guide - Core Roblox Guide - IGN
articles.summary: The Hollow Day 8 has you working your way through the movie theater's puzzle on Floor 8. You'll be completing a special puzzle at the end, and then
articles.body:
The Hollow Day 8 has you working your way through the movie theater's puzzle on Floor 8. You'll be completing a special puzzle at the end, and then you'll have a chance to complete another quest in the featured game for the day, Sonaria. Completing both tasks rewards you with a UGC reward, namely the Rotten Pumpkin and the Wings of Corrupted Jerry . In this guide, we'll be detailing a full walkthrough on how to complete the Floor 8 puzzle and how to complete the Sonaria quest in Roblox .

You can start the Hollow Day 8 maze puzzle by going to the movie theater's elevator and entering Floor 8. You'll need to navigate this to reach the Relic room. Like the other Relic rooms from the previous floors, the best way to reach it is by hugging the right side of the maze and taking as many rights as you can (avoiding the dead ends). The Relic room has always been on the right side, but the exact path of the maze does change.

You can see you've discovered the Relic room when you enter, and it has an altar to the left of the entrance. There are five different objects that you can pick up, but you can only pick up one at a time. You then need to bring them back to the maze and find the proper pedestals to put them on. The correct pedestal will have an outline of the object above it.

There's one for a bell, the potion, the lantern, the skull, and the candle. You'll need to return to the Relic room each time you place an object on a pedestal. After you've done this for all five items, you automatically get the Relic and can return to the elevator. If the monster catches you at any point during this portion, you'll need to start over from the beginning. Thankfully, the objects should not change positions, so long as you complete this maze on the same day.

The badge for completing the Floor 8 Maze automatically appears on your profile when you reach the top floor of the movie theater.

How to Complete the Sonaria Horror Escape Hollow Event

For the second part of Day 8, there's a quest for you to complete in Sonaria Horror Escape, called the Warden. You'll be making your way to the main lobby of this game and choosing the Warden mission. You can choose to do this yourself, but it is highly recommended to play with other players! You can complete it much faster alongside them, even if you're not in the same party.

You'll enter a match where you'll be choosing to play as Mylo the hunter, Vaelis the support, and Yoggy the lure.

You'll be working together through each floor to destroy the various infections that appear. You'll approach the infection sites, destroying the set amount that appear on that floor, before escaping to the door. You can do this by approaching the infection to attack it, and then rapidly clicking your attack button when the animation pops up. If you need help finding the infections, follow the red lights! These show you their exact positions.

There are enemies wandering around that you have to avoid if they get too close to you as you seek out the infections. Expect to pick up items along the way, and you should be using the items on your hot bar to increase your stamina, speed, and heal yourself.

You'll repeat this process for five floors, collecting items that you find and using your abilities. When you have other players helping you out, this part can happen pretty quickly!

After you reach round five, there's the final boss that you have to defeat the boss. Before you can get to them, there are infection sites that you need to destroy, lowering their shield.

With its shield down, the final boss appears, and you'll need to use Hollow Claws to throw at it. You need to be in range of the boss and use the item to damage it. You'll need to grab multiple of this item to do enough damage.

Once it reaches zero, you'll have defeated the boss and earned your reward! You can head back to the Hollow's lobby and receive your reward: Wings of Corrupted Jerry.

articles.title: The New Apple TV Series Nocturne Is Threading a Needle With Familiar Tropes and a Remixed Storyline
articles.summary: Review: Nocturne Episodes 1 & 2 are threading a needle as it hopes to intrigue viewers with familiar tropes delivered in a remixed storyline.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Nocturne Episodes 1 and 2, which are available on Apple TV now.

Apple TV’s new thriller series, Nocturne, aims to draw audiences in with just the right balance of the familiar and the unexpected. The show asks what happens when a boy thought to be the victim of a serial killer returns alive, and follows the criminal mastermind as he maneuvers law enforcement during their race to save any other victims who may still be out there. Over the course of these first two episodes, viewers are left with questions — a mix of plot-driven intrigue, interest in character development, and a touch of side-eye around potential logic gaps or plot conveniences.

Nocturne is based on Lars Kepler’s crime novels (The Sandman and Lazarus), and adapted by Rowan Joffe and John Hlavin for TV. These debut episodes lay the groundwork for convicted killer Jurek Walter’s unfolding scheme to free himself (he is astonishingly well played by Stephen Graham), set against multiple law enforcement officers’ attempts to a) stop him from doing more harm and b) find any of the still-living victims. Jurek was convicted of a series of brutal killings, which devastated a small town. He managed to get a jury to buy into an insanity defense, or we must presume he did, as he’s in a psychiatric hospital rather than a prison. (Side note: how he pulled that off is a nagging question, as nothing in his demeanor suggests an insanity defense would fly… If it’s simply that he’s a sociopath, wouldn’t that apply to all killers? Moving on.)

From a technical perspective, the show does a beautiful job of dropping us in this world. The opening shot of Episode 1, “Lazarus, Come Forth,” establishes a sense of foreboding, danger, and claustrophobia that will become a refrain throughout the series. We get the sense that the creature we are encountering is not unlike a lion in a cage. The camera moves down a cold, concrete hallway toward cells that feel (purposefully) hidden and forgotten — the shot is all the more suffocating because the dark walls of the cell entryways initially obscure the sides of the frame. This is our introduction to Jurek, and it’s notable that the series starts by putting us in the mindset of the killer. He feels trapped and eager to get out. For some yet-to-be-revealed purpose, his gritty, simultaneously menacing and soothing voice whispers to the patient next door, luring the man to seek freedom by any means necessary, even with violence (in this case, against himself). This is Jurek’s central arc across the first two episodes.

He is brilliant and adept at psychological warfare. He also seems to believe he’s entitled to his freedom, or at the very least that there is some legal loophole that will get his conviction overturned if only he can expose the lie that former homicide detective Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber) told to seal Jurek’s fate. Jurek taunts Jonah towards the close of the first episode with an offer of “the truth for the truth” when Jonah and Special Agent Quinn (Poorna Jagannathan, lately of Lanterns) visit him. In other words, Jurek will help them find more of his victims, specifically Felicia Frost — the missing sister of Michael, the boy who’s come back from the dead — if Jonah confesses to lying in court. This raises the stakes for everyone, including Agent Quinn, who’s already taken a risk by bringing a retired cop she doesn’t know this close to her case. If his old lie blows it up, that’s on her, with a missing girl’s life on the line.

While some crime dramas give the audience only as much information as the characters searching for answers have, this one puts the audience a step ahead. It’s an interesting choice, and may ultimately be a misdirect. Here’s what appears to have happened: a hospital worker named Karl (Rory Culkin) is assigned to the team that oversees Jurek. Their first encounter, like others in the series, is crafted with impressive tension: Karl searches for a missing weapon beneath Jurek’s metal bed, gets caught by his pant leg, and can’t free himself before Jurek comes to from a sedative — the trapped animal motif plays throughout. Before the scene is over, Jurek has pressed a note into Karl’s pocket, urging him to smuggle it out to his lawyer (more on the questions this raises in a bit).

The note Jurek hands Karl seems to set everything in motion: the strong implication is that, lawyer or no lawyer, it contained Jurek’s instruction to an accomplice to free Michael. Jonah is actively drawn back into the case when Michael turns up alive, as the children’s mother, Ida Frost (Chrissy Metz), and the residents of the town trust him more than anyone else in law enforcement. Also advocating for his participation is FBI agent Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz), his goddaughter, the child of his deceased partner, and someone he effectively raised. (She eventually goes undercover as a patient in Jurek’s secured ward in order to ascertain who is leaking messages and endangering lives.)

The reality is, Jonah has clearly never given up on finding the remaining missing persons associated with the case: as Agent Bauer discovers via his giant murder board, he’s been methodically searching an enormous grid, single-handedly, for years. The case is deeply personal for both of them. Jonah carries guilt for having quit the force after the (seemingly unrelated?) accidental death of his wife and child. And Jurek (or rather his accomplice) was responsible for kidnapping Bauer’s stepmother, Rebecca. It’s also implied that Bauer’s father committed suicide after his wife’s disappearance. Through Agent Quinn’s vocal skepticism, the show addresses the inappropriateness of having either Jonah or Bauer involved in the investigation, given their personal connections to Jurek. The story excuses the conflict of interest (not to mention that Jonah is no longer an officer of the law) by pointing to their familiarity with the case and the ticking clock on saving Felicia. The dynamics and interwoven tragedies all tied to Jurek stretch credulity, but the production value and strength of the performances are enough to keep the viewer engaged through a good deal of character, plot, and relationship table-setting. At its core, this is a battle of three savants with real stakes: two on the victims’ side, deploying their individual skills to best a mysterious, murderous genius. That brings us to the tightrope the series walks.

When crime dramas lean on preternatural intellect, whether it’s Sherlock Holmes or his foil, Moriarty, they run the risk of reading as a lazy sort of magic trick, where the detective or killer effortlessly “knows things” they’d need to in order to keep the story moving. Indeed, Jonah’s near-instant recognition of where Michael was being held, and Jurek’s Derren Brown-level ability to read people (pegging Karl’s guitar playing and Jonah’s partner’s violent alcoholism), open the door to the kind of conveniences that could lose a modern audience as the series unfolds. It already causes one to wonder: if Jurek is in possession of that kind of mental acuity, why did he get caught while his partner went free? Fortunately, Graham, who stunned the world with Adolescence last year, is deeply compelling, allowing us to give ourselves over to his performance.

That isn’t to undercut the potent talent of the rest of the cast, or the visual storytelling. The show is beautifully shot, with well-crafted production design. It immerses us in a rustic exterior world that vacillates between gray and worn, and comfortingly familiar. The forest landscapes are striking, but dense and dangerous in a way that mirrors the cold, stifling confines of the hospital Jurek is housed in.

Schreiber is delivering a grounded, understated portrayal of a grieving man who is just a bit too tired to fully fight against terrible ideas (Bauer’s undercover operation) and far too invested to stop himself from digging, with or without permission. One moment that stands out is when Agent Quinn tells Jonah she’s sorry for the loss of his wife and child; he nods, and unbearable pain flashes in his eyes for an instant before he moves on. Beetz is convincing and deeply affecting as a chameleon-like agent willing to harm herself (physically or otherwise) to close a case. It’s clear that this particular operation may drive her to a breaking point for multiple reasons: Jurek’s uncanny ability to read others and play on their weaknesses, her own stepmother’s disappearance (which he is connected to), and, not least of all, that it taps into the trauma of a woman who was the child of a mentally ill mother and addict father. That fear comes through as she prepares to enter the ward, right after visiting her mother. Beetz gives the sense that Bauer is unsure whether she’s crossing a line she won’t be able to come back from, where fact and fiction are too close. Bill Camp is also endearing as Chief Ellison, particularly as he talks about what the Frost kids meant to the town; he looks vulnerable, like a man who knows he is out over his skis, but wishes he wasn’t.

It took a moment for me to recognize Culkin as the compassionate nurse, Karl. Physically, his hair is doing a great deal to support the transformation, but this is also a side of the actor less seen on screen. There was one moment, when he first sees Jurek on the security cameras, in which I was left to wonder if he had some nefarious intent. But for the most part, he reads as a man of incredible kindness and skill with patients whom most of society writes off and exiles. That said, it’s odd that an employee who demonstrates an extraordinary amount of empathy is tapped for a job that puts him right in the crosshairs of a person known to exploit those instincts, and in a dangerous environment that requires a certain degree of toughness. Additionally, Karl, who is clearly driven by financial need (he accepts the new job the moment he’s informed that it comes with a raise and tells Jurek he can’t afford to lose it), inexplicably risks his career for a dangerous criminal he just met.

So, that leaves us with a couple of options: this is a piece of plotting that doesn’t logically track, or Karl isn’t who we think he is. If it’s the latter, perhaps Karl was “sent” into the hospital with purpose. It’s strangely convenient that Jurek’s day nurse went missing (and is likely dead), making room for Karl to take over. Theoretically, the patient who injures himself in the opening sequence could have gotten word to Jurek’s partner to get rid of the day nurse and make room for Karl. But how could Jurek have known that the exact right personality type for his purposes was working a few floors above him, let alone that he’d get the job? Was Karl a plant, then, and Jurek’s accomplice? That doesn’t square with their first encounter, where, with no witnesses, Jurek treats Karl as a stranger and insists he is still a human deserving care. And if someone else on staff was steering Karl, Jurek already has a partner on the inside, so why would he need Karl? Those are just a few of the questions that may or may not pay off at the close of the series. There are smaller dangling threads as well. For example, Jonah finds footprints both in the building where Michael was held and outside the missing day nurse’s home, so why in the world would he hold them back from the FBI? Ostensibly, he’d do anything to find Felicia, so that type of behavior simply doesn’t track. Ironically, the serial killer is doing a better job of asking for help and relying on a partner.

That said, the series works in no small part because Graham is simply impossible to look away from. He’s playing a killer who appears to have a (forgive the Dexter reference) code that makes sense to him. He says he “wants people to pay for their crimes.” Yes, that was in reference to Jonah’s “lie,” but the way he looks at the nurse who is rude to Karl reminds me of Hannibal Lecter’s deep disdain for bad manners. Graham’s depiction of Jurek is utterly magnetic and mercurial; when Jonah and Quinn visit, he breaks into a fit of giggles at the idea that she’s a “special” agent, as if the word itself is a joke, and moments later he’s commanding the room, telling them with understated menace that they’re only there because he brought them there. He really does seem to own them. The minute he’s off the screen, I crave more time with him.

This entirely serves the series, because it allows us to believe that others could fall under his spell, even Bauer, a smart, capable, stony FBI agent with oceans to lose. There is a deep irony that he’s maneuvering and clawing his way to freedom, given his brutal kill method of burying victims alive. He complains that he’s been in solitary, but his partner has kept a child in the dark so long that the boy went temporarily blind. There’s also a very small possibility that he is, in some way, innocent, and that he has been “made worse” by his circumstances. Either way, for those on both sides of the law, this is a story about freedom, loss, redemption, and revenge, and the first two episodes have given me enough to stick with it for now.

articles.title: Avatar: Seven Havens Ends Its First Season Going for the Heart... and Going Very, Very Dark Too
articles.summary: Review: Avatar: Seven Havens proves itself as a worthy successor to Last Airbender and Legend of Korra with a powerful, emotional, and thrilling final quartet of episodes.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for Avatar: Seven Havens Season 1, Episodes 10-13!

One thing that’s abundantly clear in the final four episodes of Avatar: Seven Havens “Book 1: Survival” is that between all the mysteries, theorizing, and big plot questions – how are there two Avatars? What did Korra do to cause the Cataclysm? What happened to Pavi (Saheli Khan) and Nisha’s (Aishu Devan) parents? – the far more important question is, and has always been, how this will impact the relationship between the twins? And to answer that, the finale is a heartbreaker, featuring one of the darkest, most upsetting endings in the Avatar franchise, while still somehow providing hope, heart, and above all, humor.

That’s a lot to tackle, and to be clear we do still get movement on the overarching mysteries of the series that should take us all the way through Book 4. That includes the reveal of what’s needed to heal the world… While fans sort of guessed what was going on, and there is likely much more to come, it turns out that the Seven Chakras that coincide with Seven Havens are directly tied to Pavi. Specifically, as the Faceless Queen Agam (Sakina Jaffrey) discovers during a spiritual alignment in Episode 11, “Battle of the Ruins,” Pavi’s chakras are all messed up. And once she’s able to face her fear of being revealed as the Avatar in the finale, “The Root Chakra,” she unlocks – guess what – her Root Chakra.

Both we, the audience, and Nisha are surprised that it’s Pavi who can unlock these alone; it was completely reasonable to speculate that the only way of stopping the fear literally bubbling under the Haven of Ellora was through Nisha and Pavi working together. Instead, the additional shocker is that somehow Nisha summoned that fear, killing her and Pavi’s parents in the process. Pavi was protected from the resulting rock slide by some sort of green energy, which took her leg… And Nisha, while able to hold back an energy dome about to consume the Haven in Episode 12, “The Dome,” is nowhere near as strong as Pavi, who single-handedly dispels the fear and begins to reconnect with past Avatars, as well as charting her path to her next destination, The Floating Isles (or Wilds – there are no closed captions on the screeners provided by Paramount).

(Side-note: there’s a ton of lore we could get into here, but we’ll save it for the section below.)

But in between all that, these episodes are really about two things: Pavi and Nisha, and how we react to fear. On the former, the show has managed to craft a powerful sisterly bond over the course of 13 episodes that feels real… Pavi is gutted by the revelation that Nisha killed their parents, but she’s far more upset that Nisha lied to her about it. And we’re left in a place where Pavi is finally owning up to her destiny, but seems harsher and more closed off (despite unlocking the Chakra) than the goofy weirdo who befriended rocks and bugs in the initial episodes. Meanwhile, Nisha is being cheered by the crowd in Ellora at the end, a flip on the fear of the Avatar that dogged her every move. But she’s just seen Pavi display more power than she ever has, and that clearly alarms her. They haven’t exactly changed positions, but it’s clear this resolution isn’t as simple as “hooray, fear cured!”

That gets to the second part, which we’ve been harping on all season: fear. The show hasn’t necessarily been subtle about how it’s reflecting our current world (or at least the world of several years ago when they were writing, developing, and animating this), but when a character says “We can’t just hide from this scary bubble” or “Freedom of choice is all I’ve ever wanted” they’re basically putting it out there what metaphorical levels the show is working on. And what works about it is that the series still functions as a rollicking adventure show and a sweet all-ages animated show while still being very blunt about where it leans politically.

And that’s what the best of entertainment should be doing, right? Commenting on our real world while also working as, you know, entertainment. Seven Havens has absolutely nailed that balance over 13 episodes. Not only that, but these final four address a number of fan “concerns” that have bubbled up. One of them has been about the “weak” bending, which one could venture comes from the fact that bending is disappearing from the world (as stated multiple times) and which we now know at least in part comes from these seven Chakras being blocked. But also, Pavi taking on the fear energy dome in the finale rocked . No pun intended on earthbending, but saving up your big bending stunts for the finale makes sense in terms of the build of a season.

The other question about the show has been why Pavi and Nisha are nine years old, with concerns raised that they’re trying to age down the Avatar series even further than has already happened. While one could point out here that it’s a children’s cartoon on Nickelodeon, and apologies this isn’t catering to you, an adult who watched the original series 20 years ago, this finale cemented that not only is this show going crazy dark and upsetting – with Pavi and Nisha’s parents abandoning Nisha, then dying in a rockslide caused by Nisha – but at the very least Pavi is starting to grow up by the end of the episode. Her hair is different, and Khan does a masterful job of maturing her voice. There’s been speculation about a time jump going into further seasons, and given the epic journey nature of the show (as also set up in the finale) that seems likely… They won’t be nine forever.

Okay, before we get too much farther, let’s recap the specific episodes (briefly), though they all work nicely together as a four-part finale. First up is Episode 10, “Ghosts and Spirits.” The thrust here is that Chancellor Kayoko (Jennifer Sun Bell) has been driven mad by the fear anomaly, and has the whole city under martial law. While Pavi deals with the metaphorical ghosts of her parents after discovering her childhood home, Nisha encounters the first spirit we’ve seen on the show, which leads her to the place we later discover she freaked out at and killed her parents. And in the midst of this, Agam discovers the duo and leads them to her hideout.

Then in Episode 11, “Battle of the Ruins,” Kayoko makes the exceedingly poor decision to redirect the bubbling pit of fear energy under Ellora to the hideout of the Faceless. We also discover definitively that Jae (Major Curda) never betrayed the Order of the White Lotus; he was just trying to not get arrested so he can free them later. We also get info on the Chakras from Agam, and they end up fighting the bubbling fear energy together, barely escaping in time.

Episode 12, “The Dome,” heads back to Ellora as Nisha solo tries to stop the energy, now in the form of (yep) a dome, while Pavi holds it back. Kayoko isn’t having any of it, and breaks Nisha’s hold, releasing the dome, which consumes our twins… Leading to a vision of their mother. Also, Jae and his boyfriend Datu (Topher Ngo) break up, which is a real bummer for ‘shippers but lets Jae be free to travel in the next episode.

And then we’ve got the finale, Episode 13, “The Root Chakra,” which we’ve covered a chunk of already. To touch on a few other points/where we leave folks, Pavi leaves for the next Haven with Jae by her side, while Nisha stays in Ellora with Karthik (Akshay Khanna). Kayoko is still possessed by the fear entity, which seems… interesting. Agam, meanwhile, seems to stay in Ellora, while she names Zi (Dianne Doan) the Faceless Queen, and the rest of the Faceless presumably head to Republic Forest, as planned.

So, lots more to explore when we get into Book 2, particularly with the twins separated and on very different paths. We still don’t know why or how there are two Avatars, what led to Nisha’s parents wanting to abandon her, how Korra caused the Cataclysm, or why Pavi’s Chakras are blocked. But if this first, excellent season is any indication, Books 2, 3, and 4 will all do what Book 1 did so well: lead with its heart on its sleeve.

Avatar Easter Eggs, References, and Connections

Before we get to the Easter eggs and references, it’s important to recognize the untimely, awful passing of voice actor Eric Bauza at age 46 on October 25. While Bauza didn’t voice any of the main roles on the series, he was, as always, a utility player. In these final four episodes alone he’s credited with Jin-Woo, Townsperson, Elloran Citizens, Kosal, Pich, Faceless, Faceless Bandits, Faceless Kids, Firebender, Guard #2, Benders, Guards, and Ellorans – just to give you an idea of how important this legend was to the series. And not only that, but he also stood out as Pudding Guy in the previous chunk of episodes, a delightful addition that seemed to be the heir to The Last Airbender’s Cabbage Merchant. What they’ll do with that role in subsequent seasons is TBD, but Bauza leaves a gap in the world of Avatar that can’t readily be filled.

Not to make an abrupt turn, but let’s talk about those blocked chakras. This was first introduced in The Last Airbender and explored when Aang was injured by Azula, and was unable to access the Avatar State. Here, while Pavi goes HAM on that red energy dome in the finale, she does not enter the Avatar State at all, likely because her Chakras are blocked. But we do get a strange red glow around her, and that greenish glow that protected her from Nisha’s rock slide in the flashback, which seems to be something new.

Speaking of something new, when Pavi does finally unlock her Root Chakra, she sees constellation versions of the previous Avatars Kyoshi, Roku, Aang, and finally Korra (aka, the four Avatars before Pavi and Nisha). Without getting too deep in the weeds here, at the end of Legend of Korra, thanks to a big fight between Raava and Vaatu, the spirits of order and chaos, Korra’s connection to the Avatar Cycle was severed, then begun anew. So whatever Pavi is seeing in this Rainbow Road/constellation deal is something different (or, since Korra went on many adventures after the final season of Legend of Korra, perhaps she experienced something different first).

As for Easter eggs, these episodes are remarkably light by comparison to the rest of the season, but we do have a few. Jae proudly declares “I will always be Team Avatar” in Episode 11, giving us our first glimpse of this show’s, well, Team Avatar – something we’ve gotten in both The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra.

In Episode 12, Pavi makes an absolutely ridiculous mud mask for Nisha to disguise her – which works, as an Elloran refers to her as “old man.” This is just part of a long tradition of Team Avatar having the absolute worst disguises that, somehow, beyond all reason, always actually disguise them.

And one blink and you’ll miss it Easter egg, as everyone flees the energy dome in Ellora at the beginning of Episode 13, sees a citizen quickly walk in front of the camera holding – what else – an armful of cabbages.

articles.title: Capcom Isn't Scrapping Resident Evil, but Mainline Story Could Wrap Up in Next 10 Years According to Producer
articles.summary: IGN recently reported that Resident Evil series producer Jun Takeuchi commented that Capcom’s survival horror series’ story could end in the next 10 years. However, this does not mean that Capcom plans to stop making Resident Evil games in the next decade.
articles.body:
IGN recently reported that Resident Evil series producer Jun Takeuchi commented that Capcom’s survival horror series’ story could end in the next 10 years. However, this does not mean that Capcom plans to stop making Resident Evil games in the next decade.

As Takeuchi told 47 News (picked up by Yahoo Japan ) in a recent interview, “With the release of Requiem this year, I feel like the first 10 years have reached the end of a chapter, so I think the conclusion will come in the following 10 years."

This quote set news outlets and fans wondering if Capcom plans to wind up its popular franchise by 2036. However, what Takeuchi is specifically referring to here is the company’s 10-year branding concept for the survival horror franchise. This vision kicked off with the 2019 remake of Resident Evil 2 , which Takeuchi refers to in the previous paragraph, and involved much mulling over how to deal with Resident Evil’s overarching story.

“The series' story wasn't all planned out from the beginning, it expanded with each new release," Takeuchi said. "When we were planning the Resident Evil 2 remake and coming up with the 10-year branding concept, this (the story) was what we puzzled over. If you play through all of these games, I think you'll work out the meaning behind the order of the remakes.”

Therefore, the ‘first 10 years’ Takeuchi is referring to is the decade of this branding concept. This period saw the release of the Resident Evil 2, 3 and 4 remakes, plus Village and Requiem. Another remake, Resident Evil Veronica , is due out next year. It is this overarching, mainline story that Takeuchi feels will wrap up in the upcoming decade (i.e. ‘the following 10 years’).

Takeuchi’s vision for the next decade of Resident Evil will include both remakes and new titles. However, when asked how many fresh Resi titles will be released before 2036, Takeuchi failed to spill the details but did say we can expect multiple games.

Resident Evil is one of Capcom’s top multimedia franchises (with the company's latest financial report highlighting strong ongoing sales). If this momentum continues, Capcom will likely still have other Resident Evil releases on the zombie-infested horizon in 2036 and beyond. Even if the main story concludes, there is plenty of potential for games and movies to timeline-hop or delve into new settings. Capcom could also catch up with beloved characters like Jill Valentine or Rebecca Chambers.

Resident Evil Requiem producer Masato Kumazawa mused earlier this year that the series might one day get a game set in Japan (a location that has only ever appeared in the official manga spin-off Biohazard Heavenly Island). “Even though Japan hasn’t appeared as a setting for the games yet, I think it might at some point in the future." he said, adding: "There are still many things we'd like to do."

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.
